seen.note: Why-now 2026-07-28: npm publish-time malware scanning + dual-use metadata - new package.json 'contentPolicy' field + a text-only DISCLOSURE file in the package root, 2FA-enforced publishing, and both are PERSISTENT (cannot be removed in later versions). Enforcement progressive; existing dual-use maintainers emailed. https://github.blog/changelog/2026-07-28-npm-publish-time-malware-scanning-and-dual-use-metadata/ Occupant hunt: EMPTY across 2 formulations. Day-build gate passes on mechanics (static page, no credential). REJECTED because the contentPolicy SCHEMA IS NOT PUBLISHED - a validator would invent the rules and assert them as fact, i.e. a green checkmark on a guessed rule. REVISIT TRIGGER: npm publishes the contentPolicy schema (docs.npmjs.com or the npm CLI schema).

plain.what: A checker for npm’s brand-new security paperwork: paste your package.json and it tells you whether your publish will be blocked.
plain.solves: Since 2026-07-28 npm scans every publish for malware and requires ‘dual-use’ declarations — get them wrong and your release stalls.
plain.money: Free checker → paid per-release validation in CI. NOT BUILT: npm hasn’t published the actual rules, so any verdict today would be a guess dressed as fact. Re-enters the moment the schema ships.

seen.outcome: rejected - undocumented by design; kept as a DEMAND SIGNAL
seen.note: Why-now 2026-07-28: GitHub Actions now HOLDS workflow runs identified as potentially malicious until a write-access collaborator approves; public github.com repos only, not GHES. https://github.blog/changelog/2026-07-28-github-actions-holds-potentially-malicious-workflows-for-approval/ Occupant hunt: empty (6 days old). Value retained: it ENLARGES the population asking 'why didn't my workflow run', which strengthens gha-trigger. NO REVISIT unless GitHub documents the criteria.

plain.money: None — rejected. GitHub keeps the detection rules secret on purpose, so every prediction would be guesswork. Its existence still pushes more confused people toward gha-trigger.

seen.outcome: REBUILD PICKED 2026-08-03 (Monday). Ship 002 rebuilt on a linear-time matcher.
seen.note: XSS fixed and confirmed dead; 56/56 vs GitHub cheat sheet, 0 inverted verdicts. Fails on a glob-engine ReDoS that a static complexity budget cannot bound. REVISIT AS A REBUILD, not a new candidate: replace globToRegex/gmatch with a linear-time non-backtracking matcher (two-pointer + backtrack memo, or DP), verify against the existing 56-case published oracle and the ~67M-pair differential harness.
seen.rebuild_constraint: Replace globToRegex/gmatch with a LINEAR-TIME non-backtracking matcher (two-pointer with backtrack memo, or DP over pattern x path). BORROW: port nektos/act pkg/workflowpattern (MIT, correct GitHub semantics, scores 49/49) rather than hand-roll — hand-rolling is what produced the XSS then the ReDoS. VERIFY against lib/checks/gha-filter-oracle.json (46 published pairs) + lib/checks/redos-probes.json (must resolve <50ms each, no UI freeze) + lib/checks/xss-payloads.json. Add the LIVE analytics beacon (ship 002 predates it). Kill-criterion in per-path visits, not tool-runs. [2026-08-03 CORRECTION, from reading the port source rather than trusting the plan: act is linear-time because Go's regexp is RE2, NOT because of its pattern translation. PatternToRegex emits ordinary regex text. A VERBATIM JS PORT WOULD REINTRODUCE THE ReDoS, because JS RegExp backtracks. Port act's SEMANTICS line-for-line; execute them on a Thompson NFA / Pike-VM state-set simulation, never on JS RegExp.]

plain.what: A free web page: paste your GitHub Actions workflow file, say what you pushed, and it answers WILL RUN or WON'T RUN — pointing at the exact filter line that decided it.
plain.solves: “Why didn’t my CI run?” is one of GitHub’s most-asked questions. The branch/path filter rules are fiddly, and today people debug by pushing over and over.
plain.money: Free until 2026-09-02 while the beacon counts visits. ≥300 unique visits graduates it to Sunday triage for a paid layer (e.g. the same check running inside your repo’s CI); under 300, it dies to the graveyard.
